summary.text: Introduce \(b_0=2, b_1=56\) with \(b_{n+2}=-4b_{n+1}-64b_n\); direct algebra shows both \(b_n^2\) and the odd-indexed subsequence satisfy \(x_{n+3}=-48x_{n+2}+3072x_{n+1}+262144x_n\). Their first three values agree, so three-step induction gives \(a(2n+1)=b_n^2\) for every \(n\).

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) be the integer sequence defined by
\[
a_0=-1,\qquad a_1=4,\qquad a_2=176,\qquad a_3=3136,
\]
and, for every \(r\ge 0\),
\[
a_{r+4}=-4a_{r+3}+256a_{r+1}+4096a_r.
\tag{1}
\]
We will prove that for every nonnegative integer \(n\), the odd-indexed term \(a_{2n+1}\) is a square of an integer.

Define an auxiliary integer sequence \((b_n)_{n\ge 0}\) by
\[
b_0=2,\qquad b_1=56,
\]
and
\[
b_{n+2}=-4b_{n+1}-64b_n\qquad(n\ge 0).
\tag{2}
\]
The main claim is the stronger identity
\[
a_{2n+1}=b_n^2
\tag{3}
\]
for every \(n\ge 0\). We establish recurrences of the same form for the two sides of (3), verify three initial cases, and then use induction.

First, the fourth-order recurrence for \(a\) implies a recurrence involving only terms whose indices have the same parity. We claim that for every \(r\ge 0\),
\[
a_{r+6}=-48a_{r+4}+3072a_{r+2}+262144a_r.
\tag{4}
\]
Indeed, applying (1) at indices \(r+6\) and \(r+5\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{r+6}&=-4a_{r+5}+256a_{r+3}+4096a_{r+2},\\
a_{r+5}&=-4a_{r+4}+256a_{r+2}+4096a_{r+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Substitution of the second equation into the first yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{r+6}
&=-4\bigl(-4a_{r+4}+256a_{r+2}+4096a_{r+1}\bigr)
  +256a_{r+3}+4096a_{r+2}\\
&=16a_{r+4}+3072a_{r+2}+256a_{r+3}-16384a_{r+1}.
\tag{5}
\end{aligned}
\]
On the other hand, (1) at index \(r+4\) says
\[
a_{r+4}=-4a_{r+3}+256a_{r+1}+4096a_r.
\]
Multiplying this equality by \(64\) and rearranging gives
\[
256a_{r+3}-16384a_{r+1}=-64a_{r+4}+262144a_r.
\tag{6}
\]
Inserting (6) into (5), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{r+6}
&=16a_{r+4}+3072a_{r+2}-64a_{r+4}+262144a_r\\
&=-48a_{r+4}+3072a_{r+2}+262144a_r,
\end{aligned}
\]
which proves (4).

Next we derive the corresponding recurrence for the squares of the auxiliary sequence. We claim that for every \(n\ge 0\),
\[
b_{n+3}^2=-48b_{n+2}^2+3072b_{n+1}^2+262144b_n^2.
\tag{7}
\]
Put \(x=b_n\) and \(y=b_{n+1}\). From (2),
\[
b_{n+2}=-4y-64x.
\]
Applying (2) once more,
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_{n+3}
&=-4b_{n+2}-64b_{n+1}\\
&=-4(-4y-64x)-64y\\
&=256x-48y.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
b_{n+3}^2=(256x-48y)^2
=65536x^2-24576xy+2304y^2.
\tag{8}
\]
Meanwhile,
\[
\begin{aligned}
-48b_{n+2}^2+3072b_{n+1}^2+262144b_n^2
&=-48(-4y-64x)^2+3072y^2+262144x^2\\
&=-48(16y^2+512xy+4096x^2)
  +3072y^2+262144x^2\\
&=2304y^2-24576xy+65536x^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is exactly the expression in (8), proving (7).

We now verify (3) for \(n=0,1,2\).

For \(n=0\), the definitions give
\[
a_1=4=2^2=b_0^2.
\]

For \(n=1\),
\[
a_3=3136=56^2=b_1^2.
\]

For \(n=2\), first compute \(a_4\) from (1):
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_4
&=-4a_3+256a_1+4096a_0\\
&=-4(3136)+256(4)+4096(-1)\\
&=-15616.
\end{aligned}
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_5
&=-4a_4+256a_2+4096a_1\\
&=-4(-15616)+256(176)+4096(4)\\
&=62464+45056+16384\\
&=123904.
\end{aligned}
\]
The auxiliary recurrence gives
\[
b_2=-4b_1-64b_0=-4(56)-64(2)=-352,
\]
and
\[
b_2^2=(-352)^2=123904.
\]
Thus \(a_5=b_2^2\), completing the three initial cases.

It remains to propagate the identity. Suppose for some \(n\ge 0\) that
\[
a_{2n+1}=b_n^2,\qquad
 a_{2n+3}=b_{n+1}^2,\qquad
 a_{2n+5}=b_{n+2}^2.
\tag{9}
\]
Apply the same-parity recurrence (4) with \(r=2n+1\). Since
\[
r+2=2n+3,\qquad r+4=2n+5,\qquad r+6=2n+7=2(n+3)+1,
\]
we obtain
\[
a_{2n+7}=-48a_{2n+5}+3072a_{2n+3}+262144a_{2n+1}.
\]
Using the three induction hypotheses (9), this becomes
\[
a_{2n+7}
=-48b_{n+2}^2+3072b_{n+1}^2+262144b_n^2.
\]
By the square recurrence (7), the right-hand side is \(b_{n+3}^2\). Hence
\[
a_{2(n+3)+1}=a_{2n+7}=b_{n+3}^2.
\]
Thus, whenever (3) holds at three consecutive values \(n,n+1,n+2\), it also holds at \(n+3\).

Since (3) has been proved for \(n=0,1,2\), this three-step induction proves it for every nonnegative integer \(n\). Explicitly, ordinary strong induction applies: for a given \(n\), the cases \(n=0,1,2\) are the established bases, while if \(n\ge 3\), writing \(n=m+3\), the identities at \(m,m+1,m+2\) imply the identity at \(m+3=n\).

Consequently, for every \(n\ge 0\),
\[
a_{2n+1}=b_n^2.
\]
Because every \(b_n\) is an integer, this expresses \(a_{2n+1}\) as the square of an integer. Therefore every odd-indexed term \(a(2n+1)\) is a perfect square, as claimed.
